alignment.note: Greek uses the finite paratactic construction Καὶ ἤκουσαν ('And they heard'), faithfully mirrored by the Peshitta's ܘܫܡܥܘ. The Vulgate instead employs an ablative absolute participial phrase Quo audito ('which having been heard'), a stylistic Latin subordination that collapses the conjunction and verb into a single circumstantial clause.
ἀρχιερεῖς / ܪܒܝ ܟܗܢܐ / principes sacerdotum; the Greek compound noun is rendered analytically as a construct phrase ('chiefs of the priests') in both Syriac and Latin.
καὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς / ܘܣܦܪܐ / et scribæ.

Greek joins with καὶ ἐζήτουν ('and they were seeking'), and the Peshitta renders the imperfect periphrastically with ܒܥܝܢ ܗܘܘ ('were seeking'). The Vulgate drops the connective and uses a simple imperfect quærebant, leaving the coordinating conjunction untranslated.
αὐτὸν ἀπολέσωσιν / ܢܘܒܕܘܢܝܗܝ / eum perderent; Syriac expresses the object pronoun as an enclitic suffix on the verb.

The high point (·) following ἀπολέσωσιν in the Greek and the colon (:) in the Vulgate both mark a strong clausal break before the explanatory γάρ/enim clause; the Syriac carries no corresponding punctuation token.
ἐφοβοῦντο / ܕܚܠܝܢ ܗܘܘ / timebant; the Peshitta again uses the periphrastic imperfect with auxiliary ܗܘܘ.
αὐτόν / ܡܢܗ / eum; Syriac uses the prepositional form ܡܢܗ ('of/from him') with the verb of fearing.

The Greek again uses postpositive γάρ to introduce the second causal clause, whereas both the Peshitta ܡܛܠ and the Vulgate quoniam employ an explicit subordinating causal conjunction ('because'), heightening the logical subordination that the Greek leaves paratactic.
πᾶς ὁ ὄχλος / ܕܟܠܗ ܥܡܐ / universa turba ('all the crowd'); the Syriac uses ܥܡܐ ('people') where Greek and Latin use the more neutral 'crowd'.

ἐξεπλήσσετο / ܬܡܝܗܝܢ ܗܘܘ / admirabatur; Greek and Latin render the verb as singular agreeing with the collective subject, while Syriac uses the plural periphrastic ('were astonished'), an idiomatic constructio ad sensum with the collective 'people'.
ἐπὶ τῇ διδαχῇ αὐτοῦ / ܒܝܘܠܦܢܗ / super doctrina ejus; Syriac compresses the prepositional phrase and possessive suffix into the single inflected form ܒܝܘܠܦܢܗ ('at his teaching').
